gateway.text:
The immune system does not recognize “cancer” as one universal label. It detects unusual signals on or around cells.

For conventional T cells, a cancer cell’s proteins can be broken into short fragments called **peptides**. **HLA** molecules display those fragments on the cell surface, like holding up small samples for inspection. A T-cell receptor (TCR) checks the combined **peptide–HLA** surface—not the peptide alone. A tumor-specific change may create a **neoantigen**, a new potential target. But the target must be produced, displayed, and recognized by a matching T cell. [TCR recognition](/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/t-cell-receptor/#the-intuition)

[[visual:1]]

In this cartoon, the cancer-immunity cycle is shown as linked jobs: tumor material becomes available, immune cells display it, T cells are activated, travel into the tumor, recognize susceptible cells, and kill them; the process can repeat. [Cancer-immunity cycle](/education/concepts/immunology/tumor-immunology/cancer-immunity-cycle/#how-it-works)

Other immune cells use different rules. Natural killer cells weigh activating signals against inhibitory “self” signals; reduced HLA display can create a possible “missing-self” signal, but it does not guarantee killing. [NK recognition](/education/concepts/immunology/innate-and-unconventional-cells/nk-cell-and-missing-self/#how-it-works)

Would you like to explore **T-cell recognition**, **NK-cell recognition**, or **how tumors escape detection** next?
